summary_responses.response: Researchers propose DiffTry (Differential Retries), a simple mechanism that transforms retries into a prioritization tool by giving high-priority microservice requests more retry attempts than low-priority ones. The approach targets temporary overloads caused by miscoordinated autoscaling, where current priority-blind retries fail to protect valuable transactions and can trigger large-scale retry storms that waste capacity and increase cost. DiffTry operates locally at the retry decision point without overload sensing or coordination between services, remaining effectively silent under normal load and activating only when rejections occur. The authors present a fluid and queueing-based analysis for a single service and extend it to general service networks with iterative equations for per-class rejection rates, proving monotonicity and convergence guarantees that ensure high-priority success rates improve with larger retry budgets. Simulations and a live Kubernetes deployment using a drop-in service-mesh plugin confirm the theory, showing for example high-priority rejection dropping to around 15% and high-priority transactions accounting for about 85% of completions despite equal input shares.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: DiffTry (Differential Retries) is a stateless mechanism that assigns different retry-attempt limits to different priority classes of requests to achieve differentiation in rejection rates.
Under overload with DiffTry, high-priority requests achieve a rejection rate of around 15% and account for about 85% of successful completions when both classes contribute 50% of input load.
DiffTry requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination and is implemented as a drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application code changes.

The paper develops an analytical model for DiffTry starting with two services in tandem, then generalizes it to networks of services using an open-network model combined with flow classes and priorities.

The paper proves that network-wide class-level success rates increase monotonically with retry limits and validates the analysis on a live Kubernetes deployment where measured rejection closely matches the theoretical predictions.
DiffTry assigns different retry attempt limits to requests from different priority classes to prioritize high-value transactions during overload.

summary_responses.response: The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD 2026-20-09), effective November 18, 2026, for certain Bombardier Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes. The rule was prompted by Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 reporting low clearance in the right wing between the fuel line flexible coupling and harness support bracket clip-nut in bay 3, between the fuel coupling and hydraulic system 3 line in bay 18, and between hydraulic lines and fuel vent tube in bay 20, which could create an ignition source in the fuel tank during a lightning strike. The AD requires replacing the clip-nut and fuel tube assemblies to rectify the first two clearance issues, plus inspecting the hydraulic-to-vent-tube clearance and replacing hydraulic support brackets if needed. The FAA declined requests for an emergency AD, shorter compliance time, or reopened comment period, stating the condition would not cause fuel starvation, no system failure analysis was needed, and the Transport Canada compliance times and costs were adequate and reasonably available. The agency estimates the AD affects 60 US-registered airplanes at about $2,693 per aircraft ($161,580 total), with potential additional on-condition costs of $5,772 per aircraft, some possibly covered under warranty.

summary_responses.response:
The Office of Personnel Management has issued a direct final rule updating its Family and Medical Leave Act regulations to reflect statutory changes enacted in January 2021 and December 2023.
The rule is scheduled to take effect December 14, 2026 unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026.
The January 2021 amendments exclude Veterans Health Administration employees covered under a separate leave system from title 5 FMLA coverage, expand the 12-month service requirement to include virtually all federal civilian service including temporary, intermittent, Postal Service and nonappropriated fund employment, and clarify that annual and sick leave earned outside title 5 may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave.
The December 2023 amendment further expands eligibility by allowing honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force or Marine Corps to count toward the 12-month requirement.
Because paid parental leave requires FMLA eligibility, these changes also broaden access to paid parental leave and the rule codifies guidance previously issued in OPM policy memoranda.
